You are working on the Obsidian plugin that implements the Discourse Graph protocol.

## Dependencies

Prefer existing dependencies from package.json.

## Obsidian Style Guide

Use the obsidian style guide from help.obsidian.md/style-guide and docs.obsidian.md/Developer+policies.

### Icons

Platform-native UI.
Lucide and custom Obsidian icons can be used alongside detailed elements to provide a visual representation of a feature.

Example: In the ribbon on the left, select Create new canvas ( lucide-layout-dashboard.svg > icon ) to create a canvas in the same folder as the active file.

Guidelines for icons

Store icons in the Attachments/icons folder.
Add the prefix lucide- before the Lucide icon name.
Add the prefix obsidian-icon- before the Obsidian icon name.
Example: The icon for creating a new canvas should be named lucide-layout-dashboard.

Use the SVG version of the icons available.
Icons should be 18 pixels in width, 18 pixels in height, and have a stroke width of 1.5. You can adjust these settings in the SVG data.
Adjusting size and stroke in an SVG.
Utilize the icon anchor in embedded images, to tweak the spacing around the icon so that it aligns neatly with the text in the vicinity.
Icons should be surrounded by parenthesis. ( lucide-cog.svg > icon )
Example: ( ![[lucide-cog.svg#icon]] )

### Function guides

- Any function that deals with querying vault's frontmatter, default to using Datacore API first, then write fallback where you use `plugin.app.vault.getMarkdownFiles()` to iterate through each file's frontmatter

## Plugin Store Guidelines

These rules must be followed for the plugin to be accepted into the Obsidian community plugin store.

### Security

- Never use `innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, or `insertAdjacentHTML` with user-controlled content
- Use Obsidian DOM helpers instead: `createEl()`, `createDiv()`, `createSpan()`

### App instance

- Always use `this.app` — never the global `app` object

### Event listeners

- Register all event listeners via `this.registerEvent()` so they are automatically cleaned up on plugin unload

### UI text

- Use sentence case in settings headings and labels (not title case)
- Prefer `setHeading()` over raw HTML heading elements (`<h1>`, `<h2>`, etc.)

### Commands

- Do not set default hotkeys — they conflict with other plugins
- Use the correct callback type: `callback` for always-available commands, `checkCallback` when the command is conditionally available, or the editor variants for editor-scoped commands
- Do not manually prepend the plugin ID to command IDs — Obsidian adds it automatically

### Workspace

- Do not store references to custom views — look them up fresh each time they are needed
  Don't do this:
  `this.registerView(MY_VIEW_TYPE, () => this.view = new MyCustomView());`
  Do this instead:
  `this.registerView(MY_VIEW_TYPE, () => new MyCustomView());`
  To access the view from your plugin, use `Workspace.getActiveLeavesOfType():`

```
for (let leaf of app.workspace.getActiveLeavesOfType(MY_VIEW_TYPE)) {
  let view = leaf.view;
  if (view instanceof MyCustomView) {
    // ...
  }
}
```

- Do not detach leaves during plugin unload

### Editor

- Prefer the Editor API over `Vault.modify()` when the note is currently open in the editor
- Prefer `Vault.process()` instead of `Vault.modify()` to modify a file in the background

### Mobile compatibility

- Node.js and Electron APIs (`fs`, `crypto`, `os`) are unavailable on mobile
- If the plugin targets mobile, use web API equivalents: `SubtleCrypto` instead of `crypto`, `navigator.clipboard` for clipboard access
- Regex lookbehind assertions are not supported on some mobile — avoid them if possible

### Code quality

- Use `const`/`let` — never `var`
- Prefer `async`/`await` over `.then()` chains
- Minimize `console.log` — remove debug logs before shipping
- Do not hardcode styles inline — use CSS classes and Obsidian's CSS variables

## Unit tests

Vitest runs the plugin's pure logic in a Node environment: `pnpm test:unit` (or `pnpm test:watch` while working). The repository-wide `pnpm ci:validate` picks it up through the `test:unit` script.

- Put tests in `src/**/__tests__/<module>.test.ts`, next to the code they cover. Tests covering the test scaffolding itself live in `test/`; those two globs are the whole of `include` in `vitest.config.mts`.
- Import the module under test through the `~` alias, as the source does.
- `obsidian` ships type declarations with no runtime entry point, so `vitest.config.mts` aliases it to `test/obsidianStub.ts`. Add to that stub whatever a new test needs to load its module; use `vi.mock("obsidian")` in the test itself when the test needs to assert on a call.
- Obsidian's own objects are large. Build the slice the code path reads and cast it (`{ metadataCache: … } as unknown as App`) rather than constructing a whole `App` or `TFile`.
- Logic that needs a live vault, editor, or workspace is not covered here — extract the decision into a util and test that.

### Keeping the stub honest

The stub is hand-written, so it can be wrong about the API today and can fall behind when the `obsidian` dependency is bumped. Two mechanisms catch that. Each runs under exactly one command, so run `pnpm ci:validate` to get both.

`test/obsidianStub.conformance.ts` type-checks each stub member against the real declaration. It is type-only and matches none of the vitest globs, so only `pnpm check-types` enforces it. Keep it inside the `tsconfig.json` include, or the drift check disappears with no signal.

- Members with real behavior are fully conformant.
- Shells, which exist only so an importing module loads, are checked for the export name alone. When a shell gains behavior, move it to the conformant group.
- Every export must appear in one group or the other, so adding one without classifying it fails the build.

`test/obsidianStub.test.ts` pins the behavior the stub reimplements, which the type checker cannot see. It is type-checked like any other file, but only `pnpm test:unit` runs its assertions.

### Verifying the stub

Type declarations cannot tell you what a function returns for a given input, so do not guess it. Obsidian ships its implementation in `obsidian.asar`, in the resources directory of the installed app, and the current cases were settled by reading it. Two details it settled: `normalizePath("/")` returns `"/"`, and `TFolder.isRoot()` tests `path === "/"` rather than a null parent.

The bundle is minified, so it takes two steps: find the exported name to learn its minified name, then find that function. The example below is a macOS path; on Windows and Linux locate `obsidian.asar` under the install directory and substitute it.

```
node -e 'const s=require("fs").readFileSync("/Applications/Obsidian.app/Contents/Resources/obsidian.asar","utf8");
  const i=s.indexOf("normalizePath:()=>");
  console.log(s.slice(i, i+80));'
```

Read the behavior and reimplement it; do not paste the bundle's code into this repository. Pin whatever you learn in `obsidianStub.test.ts`, and name the test `diverges: …` when the stub deliberately does something else.

- Prefer the Editor API over `Vault.modify()` when the note is currently open in the editor
- Prefer `Vault.process()` instead of `Vault.modify()` to modify a file in the background

### Mobile compatibility

- Node.js and Electron APIs (`fs`, `crypto`, `os`) are unavailable on mobile
- If the plugin targets mobile, use web API equivalents: `SubtleCrypto` instead of `crypto`, `navigator.clipboard` for clipboard access
- Regex lookbehind assertions are not supported on some mobile — avoid them if possible

### Code quality

- Use `const`/`let` — never `var`
- Prefer `async`/`await` over `.then()` chains
- Minimize `console.log` — remove debug logs before shipping
- Do not hardcode styles inline — use CSS classes and Obsidian's CSS variables

## Unit tests

Vitest runs the plugin's pure logic in a Node environment: `pnpm test:unit` (or `pnpm test:watch` while working). The repository-wide `pnpm ci:validate` picks it up through the `test:unit` script.

- Put tests in `src/**/__tests__/<module>.test.ts`, next to the code they cover. Tests covering the test scaffolding itself live in `test/`; those two globs are the whole of `include` in `vitest.config.mts`.
- Import the module under test through the `~` alias, as the source does.
- `obsidian` ships type declarations with no runtime entry point, so `vitest.config.mts` aliases it to `test/obsidianStub.ts`. Add to that stub whatever a new test needs to load its module; use `vi.mock("obsidian")` in the test itself when the test needs to assert on a call.
- Obsidian's own objects are large. Build the slice the code path reads and cast it (`{ metadataCache: … } as unknown as App`) rather than constructing a whole `App` or `TFile`.
- Logic that needs a live vault, editor, or workspace is not covered here — extract the decision into a util and test that.

### Keeping the stub honest

The stub is hand-written, so it can be wrong about the API today and can fall behind when the `obsidian` dependency is bumped. Two mechanisms catch that. Each runs under exactly one command, so run `pnpm ci:validate` to get both.

`test/obsidianStub.conformance.ts` type-checks each stub member against the real declaration. It is type-only and matches none of the vitest globs, so only `pnpm check-types` enforces it. Keep it inside the `tsconfig.json` include, or the drift check disappears with no signal.

- Members with real behavior are fully conformant.
- Shells, which exist only so an importing module loads, are checked for the export name alone. When a shell gains behavior, move it to the conformant group.
- Every export must appear in one group or the other, so adding one without classifying it fails the build.

`test/obsidianStub.test.ts` pins the behavior the stub reimplements, which the type checker cannot see. It is type-checked like any other file, but only `pnpm test:unit` runs its assertions.

### Verifying the stub

Type declarations cannot tell you what a function returns for a given input, so do not guess it. Obsidian ships its implementation in `obsidian.asar`, in the resources directory of the installed app, and the current cases were settled by reading it. Two details it settled: `normalizePath("/")` returns `"/"`, and `TFolder.isRoot()` tests `path === "/"` rather than a null parent.

The bundle is minified, so it takes two steps: find the exported name to learn its minified name, then find that function. The example below is a macOS path; on Windows and Linux locate `obsidian.asar` under the install directory and substitute it.

```
node -e 'const s=require("fs").readFileSync("/Applications/Obsidian.app/Contents/Resources/obsidian.asar","utf8");
  const i=s.indexOf("normalizePath:()=>");
  console.log(s.slice(i, i+80));'
```

Read the behavior and reimplement it; do not paste the bundle's code into this repository. Pin whatever you learn in `obsidianStub.test.ts`, and name the test `diverges: …` when the stub deliberately does something else.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/trang.doan/.claude/skills/dg-obsidian-cdp-verify

# Obsidian CDP verify

## The one command

From the worktree root:

```sh
node ~/.claude/skills/dg-obsidian-cdp-verify/scripts/run.mjs \
  --slot 1 --marker "<string only this change's bundle contains>" \
  --scenario path/to/scenarios.mjs [--scenario more.mjs] [--port 9222] [--skip-build]
```

It runs doctor → launch → deliver → scenarios → cleanup and prints the `last-run.json` path, the scenario matrix, and the `pr-evidence` args. Exit codes: 0 all pass, 1 failure, 2 vault locked, 3 marker missing.

Write scenario files in the session scratchpad, not the repo.

## Launch

- Slots come from `OBSIDIAN_VERIFY_VAULTS` in `<worktree>/apps/obsidian/.env`. It takes a JSON array or a comma list of plugin dirs or vault roots. `--slot N` is 1-based and defaults to 1.
- If Obsidian is running on the debug port, the script attaches.
- If it's running without the port, the script quits Obsidian and relaunches it with `--remote-debugging-port`. Trang approved this; the windows come back.
- If it isn't running, the script launches it with the port.
- It then opens the slot vault through `obsidian://open?path=` and waits for a page target where `.workspace` exists and `app.vault.adapter.basePath` matches the vault.
- It writes the lock `<vault>/.obsidian/dg-verify.lock` (`{pid, branch, startedAt}`) and releases it in `finally`.

## Doctor

`scripts/doctor.mjs [--slot N]` is read-only and prints JSON: the resolved slot, the lock and the Obsidian state. If another live run holds the lock, it exits 2 and asks you to switch slot. A lock left by a dead pid is ignored.

## Deliver

`scripts/deliver.mjs --marker <str>` also runs on its own.

1. `OBSIDIAN_PLUGIN_PATH=<slot plugin dir> tsx scripts/build.ts` runs once in `apps/obsidian`. It also writes `apps/obsidian/dist`, which is gitignored.
2. It greps the vault's `main.js` for `--marker` and fails if the marker is absent.
3. It reloads the plugin. The plugin id and folder are resolved from the manifests.
4. It greps again.
5. It warns about competing `dev.ts`/esbuild watchers. Your own worktree's watcher counts too, if it mirrors into the same vault.

The harness also hashes `main.js` before and after the scenarios. If it changed, the run is marked invalid.

## Drive: scenario contract

A module's `export default` is one scenario or an array of them:

```js
export default {
  name: "Search modal renders",                 // matrix row + screenshot name
  input: "run open-node-search",                // matrix text
  expected: "modal with a textbox and footer",  // matrix text
  setup: async (ctx) => ({ /* state; snapshot anything you change */ }),  // optional
  run: async ({ client, json, vault }, state) => {
    await client.evaluate(`return app.commands.executeCommandById(${json(`${vault.pluginId}:open-node-search`)});`);
    await client.waitFor(`!!document.querySelector(".dg-node-search-modal [role=textbox]")`);
    return client.evaluate(`document.querySelectorAll(".dg-search-footer-action").length`);
  },
  expect: (actual, state) => ({ pass: actual > 0, actual: `${actual} footer actions` }),  // or a boolean
  teardown: async (ctx, state) => {},           // optional: restore what setup changed
};
```

- `ctx` has `client`, `vault` (`root`, `pluginId`, `pluginDir`), `branch`, `json`, `verifyPath(name)` and `writeNote(name, body)`. `writeNote` creates or overwrites `_verify/<branch>/<name>` and returns its path.
- `client` has `evaluate`, `waitFor`, `key`, `typeText`, `pressEscape`, `screenshot`, `reloadPlugin`, `clearModals` and `send` (raw CDP).
- The harness does these for you:
  - Before each scenario, it clears modals and restores the layout captured at the start of the run.
  - After `run`, it takes a screenshot.
  - A thrown error becomes a failing row.
- The worked example is `examples/insert-link-at-cursor.mjs` (ENG-2114, 3 scenarios).

## Evidence

- The artifacts go to `<worktree>/local/obsidian-cdp/artifacts/<branch>/<runStamp>/`: `<n>-<slug>.png` and `last-run.json` (`results[]` of `{scenario, input, expected, actual, pass, screenshot}`).
- Paste the printed matrix into create-pr's Evidence section.
- Upload the screenshots with pr-evidence, using the printed args:

```sh
./apps/roam/node_modules/.bin/tsx ~/.claude/skills/pr-evidence/upload.ts --harness obsidian-cdp <printed args>
```

## Cleanup

- Cleanup dismisses modals (Escape, then force-removes leftover `.modal-container`), restores the baseline layout and releases the lock.
- **It never deletes folders or notes.** `_verify/<branch>/` persists, and reruns overwrite its notes.
- Scenarios that change vault or app settings must restore them in `teardown`.

## Gotchas

These are the ones the code can't handle for you.

| Symptom | Cause / fix |
| --- | --- |
| Double-handled keypress | Pass `type` to `client.key` only through its loop. Never send your own `keyDown`. |
| `editor.hasFocus()` false while focus looks right | This can't be measured over CDP. Assert the consequence instead, e.g. the cursor moved past the inserted text. |
| File content assertion fails, editor looks right | Saves are debounced (about 2s). `waitFor` on `app.vault.read(...)`, and don't read once. |
| `getLeaf(true)` throws "No tab group found" | Every markdown leaf was detached. Use `getLeaf("tab")`. |
| Top-level `await` throws in `evaluate` | Bodies run in a plain function. Return an async IIFE or a promise chain. |
| `iterateRootLeaves` count caps at 2 | A truthy callback return stops the iteration. Use a block body `{ n++; }`. |
| Escape handler in a modal child never wins | Obsidian's modal scope runs first. Push a `Scope` with `app.keymap.pushScope`. |
| Styling CodeMirror spans disappears on focus or scroll | Use a CM6 decoration, not MutationObserver stamping. A widget's `ignoreEvent()` must stay `true` for clicks. |
| Selectors from an old ENG example don't match | The UI drifts. The node search input is now a contenteditable `[role=textbox]`, not an `<input>`. |
| Flaky failure that looks like a code bug | Trang may be using the app mid-run. Rerun before believing a single observation. |
| Timers stall, writes land minutes late | Focus emulation normally prevents this. If it recurs, check `document.visibilityState` and ask Trang to show the window. |
| zsh eats `${VAR}` in `node -e` | Write scenarios to `.mjs` files. |

cd /Users/trang.doan/Desktop/code/discourse-graph/.claude/worktrees/eng-2228-add-link-support-to-tldraw-text-shapes-in-obsidian
git commit -q -F - <<'MSG'
Store text-shape links in meta and render them from an overlay

Michael asked us to compare meta.url against the props schema change before
committing to it, and to see how much stock tldraw we could reuse. Both point
the same way.

meta is validated as T.jsonValue, so existing canvases load untouched: the
migration, the schema fallback and its two call sites are gone, along with the

input.command:
cd /Users/trang.doan/Desktop/code/discourse-graph/.claude/worktrees/eng-2228-add-link-support-to-tldraw-text-shapes-in-obsidian
gh pr comment 1442 --body "@mdroidian Reworked in 18080b47 — took both suggestions, with one correction to the reasoning and one thing that went further than you asked.

**1. meta.url — adopted, but not for the reason given.** You were right that it keeps the props schema and avoids backfilling. You were backwards on \"reduces custom code we maintain\": \`props.url\` is precisely the key that unlocks tldraw's stock link UI, since \`useHasLinkShapeSelected\` gates on \`'url' in shape.props\`. Moving to meta forfeits the menu item, the gate and the placement, and nets only ~60 lines lighter.

What actually decided it is compatibility. With \`props.url\`, a canvas written by the new build and opened by an **older** build throws \`Unexpected property: url\` and renders a **blank canvas**. With \`meta.url\` it loads, ignores the link, and round-trips it intact on save. Canvas files are markdown synced between machines on different plugin versions, so that outweighed the menu-UX fidelity. → \`relationInstanceId\` is already stored in \`shape.meta\` on arrow shapes, so this follows existing precedent.

**2. Reusing stock components via a patch — partly.** \`patches/tldraw@3.14.2.patch\` is two lines making \`useHasLinkShapeSelected\` also accept text shapes, which buys back the stock **Edit link** item in its stock position in all three menus. Worth flagging: it accepts text shapes *unconditionally*, the way geo qualifies through a \`props.url\` that defaults to \`\"\"\`. My first cut gated on \`meta.url\` being present and you could never add a *first* link — caught in verification.

Two caveats on patching. Upstream has already refactored this check into \`utils/shapes/shapes.ts\`, so the patch will break on the next tldraw bump — loudly, since \`allowUnusedPatches: false\`. And the embed-hostname patch you're thinking of (79322e44) was deleted by the very next tldraw upgrade in 278324c6, so one version is the realistic lifetime. It's isolated: drop the patch and hand-build the menu item (~40 lines) and nothing else changes.

I did **not** patch the URL validator to accept \`obsidian://\` for geo as well. It would work — \`validLinkProtocols\` is one Set, and it would fix the stock dialog for free — but \`T.linkUrl\` is protocol-only, so a patch there would admit *any* \`obsidian:\` URI including \`advanced-uri?commandid=\`, which is a one-click command-execution path from a shared canvas. Happy to do it if you want the geo consistency; it needs the check body patched, not just the Set.

**3. A third change you didn't ask for.** Trang suggested rendering the icon from \`InFrontOfTheCanvas\` like the Relations panel, rather than subclassing the text shape. That turned out to be the bigger win: the custom shape util is gone entirely, so stock tldraw text shapes are never touched. Trade-offs: the icon doesn't rotate with the shape, isn't clipped by a frame, and draws above shapes stacked over the text.

**4. Click behaviour — you were right that it was wrong.** Nodes used cmd+click → new tab while text links used cmd+click → sidebar. Now aligned: plain → sidebar, cmd → new tab, cmd+alt → split, and \`selectNone()\` after opening to match \`TldrawViewComponent\`. Non-\`obsidian:\` URLs keep stock anchor behaviour, so there are still two grammars on one icon — called out in the code.

Verified in a real vault over CDP, 5/5: toolbar-created text shape stays stock (\`meta=[]\`, no \`url\` in props), Edit link appears, icon renders and is clickable, gestures match nodes, and the link survives close/reopen with \`meta=[\"https://persist.example.com\"] props=[null] sequence=null\`.

Still open: the Loom is Trang's to record, and **Convert To drops the link** under both designs (\`convertToDiscourseNode\` builds a fresh shape and copies neither props nor meta) — pre-existing, and your Loom list walks right through it.

Given the patch dies on the next tldraw bump either way — would you rather keep it for stock menu placement, or drop it and own ~40 lines of menu item?" 2>&1 | tail -2

input.command:
cd /Users/trang.doan/Desktop/code/discourse-graph/.claude/worktrees/eng-2228-add-link-support-to-tldraw-text-shapes-in-obsidian
cat .github/pull_request_template.md > /tmp/tpl.md 2>/dev/null && echo "template read"
cat > /tmp/pr-body-1442.md <<'MD'
## Reviewer brief

**Result:** A text shape can carry a link — a web/mailto URL or an `obsidian://open` page link — with the same **Edit link** action and corner affordance as a geo shape. The link survives closing and reopening the canvas.

**Review focus:**

- **The link lives in `shape.meta.url`, not in the props schema.** `meta` is validated as `T.jsonValue`, so existing canvases load untouched — no migration, no schema change. The deciding argument is compatibility, not code volume: with `props.url`, a file written by this build and opened by an **older** build throws `Unexpected property: url` and renders a blank canvas; with `meta.url` it loads, ignores the link, and round-trips it intact. Canvas files are markdown synced between machines on different plugin versions. Precedent: `relationInstanceId` already lives in `shape.meta` on arrow shapes.
- **The icon is a canvas overlay, not a custom shape util.** `TextLinkOverlay` sits in `InFrontOfTheCanvas` beside the existing Relations and DragHandle overlays, so tldraw's text shape is never subclassed. Accepted trade-offs: the icon does not rotate with a rotated shape, is not clipped by an enclosing frame, and draws above shapes stacked over the text.
- **`patches/tldraw@3.14.2.patch` is two lines** making `useHasLinkShapeSelected` accept text shapes, which restores the stock **Edit link** item in all three menus. It accepts them *unconditionally* — the way geo qualifies via a `props.url` defaulting to `""`. Gating on `meta.url` being present instead made the first link unaddable; caught in verification.
- **`meta` is unvalidated, so the URL allowlist is applied on read** (`getTextShapeLinkUrl`), not at load. The affordance renders `<a href>`, so this is the only thing standing between a hand-edited canvas and a `javascript:` sink. Only `obsidian://open` with a `file` param is accepted — a bare `obsidian:` check would admit action URIs like `advanced-uri?commandid=`.
- **Click gestures now match discourse nodes**: plain → sidebar, cmd → new tab, cmd+alt → split.

**Risk / follow-up:**

- The patch **will** break on the next tldraw bump — upstream has already refactored this check into `utils/shapes/shapes.ts`. It fails loudly (`allowUnusedPatches: false`). The embed-hostname patch (79322e44) survived exactly one tldraw version before 278324c6 deleted it. Dropping the patch costs ~40 lines of hand-built menu item and changes nothing else.
- `obsidian://` is **not** accepted for geo shapes. Patching `validLinkProtocols` would fix that and free the stock dialog, but it is protocol-only, so it would admit any `obsidian:` action URI. Deliberately skipped.
- **Convert To drops the link** — `convertToDiscourseNode` builds a fresh shape and copies neither props nor meta. Pre-existing under both designs.
- **No unit tests**, at the author's request; the ticket's "unit tests cover link persistence and the text-shape eligibility behavior" is therefore unmet.

## Verification

`pnpm ci:validate` green, re-run with `--force` so a warm turbo cache could not mask a failure. Types, lint and build clean; lint checked for new *warnings* on added lines, not just errors.

Driven in a real vault over CDP via `dg-obsidian-cdp-verify` (slot 3), 5/5 passing:

| Scenario | Actual |
| --- | --- |
| Toolbar text shape is untouched stock | `props=[autoSize,color,font,richText,scale,size,textAlign,w] meta=[]` |
| Edit link appears for a text shape | Edit link present |
| Overlay icon renders beside the text | 1 icon, `clearOfText=true`, `centred=true` |
| Click opens the page, Cmd+click opens a new tab | plain click opened the target; root leaves 1→2 on Cmd+click |
| Link persists with no migration sequence | `meta=["https://persist.example.com"] props=[null] sequence=null iconsAfterReopen=1` |

The last row is the rework's whole point: the saved markdown carries the link in `meta`, leaves `props.url` absent, and records no migration sequence — which is what makes an older build able to open the file.

## Scope check

- [x] Ran `$scope-check` against the ENG ticket and final diff.
- Scope beyond `Done When`: **`obsidian://` page-link support**, and **click-gesture alignment with discourse nodes**. The ticket lists "a page picker or a new link format" as out of scope, but its Problem statement names page links as the primary target, and `T.linkUrl` (http/https/mailto only) cannot express one. No page picker was added. The gesture alignment was requested in review.

## Local delegated full review

- [x] Ran a comprehensive review of the entire final diff in a subagent with a fresh context.

The earlier review of the props-based implementation found an `obsidian:` fall-through to the OS handler, dropped `edit-link` guards, an invalid-Enter write and a geo-facing hint string — all fixed before this rework. The rework then removed the migration and schema-fallback code that review had also flagged.

- `obsidian://` is **not** accepted for geo shapes. Patching `validLinkProtocols` would fix that and free the stock dialog, but it is protocol-only, so it would admit any `obsidian:` action URI. Deliberately skipped.

- **No unit tests**, at the author's request; the ticket's "unit tests cover link persistence and the text-shape eligibility behavior" is therefore unmet.

`pnpm ci:validate` green, re-run with `--force` so a warm turbo cache could not mask a failure. Types, lint and build clean; lint checked for new *warnings* on added lines, not just errors.

| Scenario | Actual |
| --- | --- |
| Toolbar text shape is untouched stock | `props=[autoSize,color,font,richText,scale,size,textAlign,w] meta=[]` |

No page picker was added. The gesture alignment was requested in review.

The earlier review of the props-based implementation found an `obsidian:` fall-through to the OS handler, dropped `edit-link` guards, an invalid-Enter write and a geo-facing hint string — all fixed before this rework. Pushed and triaged. Status:

## PR [#1442](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1442) — reworked in `18080b47`

**CI:** 6 passing, 1 pending, 0 failing. **Mergeable**, but still `CHANGES_REQUESTED` — only Michael can clear that, so the PR stays blocked on his re-review.

**What changed.** The link now lives in `shape.meta.url` on the stock text shape, and the icon renders from a canvas overlay beside the existing Relations and DragHandle overlays. That deleted the custom shape util, `baseShapeUtils`, the migration, and the schema-fallback plumbing — so `canvasFileSync.ts` and `tldraw.ts` are now byte-identical to main, which is the cleanest possible answer to all three of Michael's inline comments. A two-line `patches/tldraw@3.14.2.patch` keeps tldraw's own **Edit link** item.

**Verification found a real bug in my own patch.** My first version gated on `meta.url` being present, which meant the menu item only appeared for shapes that *already had* a link — you could never add the first one. Geo avoids this because `props.url` defaults to `""`. Fixed by making text shapes unconditionally eligible. That's exactly the class of thing static checks can't catch.

CDP run is 5/5, and the row that matters: `meta=["https://persist.example.com"] props=[null] sequence=null` — no new prop, no migration sequence, which is what lets an older build open the file instead of rendering blank.

**Two things I pushed back on rather than just doing:**

- Michael's "meta reduces custom code" reasoning is backwards — `props.url` is what unlocks the stock UI, and meta forfeits it. I said so, and adopted meta on the compatibility argument instead.
- I did **not** patch the URL validator to give geo `obsidian://` support. It would work, but `T.linkUrl` is protocol-only, so it would admit `obsidian://advanced-uri?commandid=…` — a one-click command-execution path from a shared canvas. Offered it as a follow-up with the check body patched instead.

**Still open:** the Loom is yours to record; `Convert To` drops the link under both designs (pre-existing); and no unit tests, per your call — the read-time URL guard is now the only thing protecting the `href` sink.

Two lessons worth encoding, both of which cost time today — want me to save either to memory?

1. **`dg-obsidian-cdp-verify` contract** — `evaluate()` treats any expression containing `return` as a raw body (so a bare IIFE silently yields `undefined`), `waitFor()` only succeeds on a literal `true`, and `key()` takes an options object. Getting these wrong failed all 5 scenarios identically, which looks like a code bug.
2. **`pnpm patch-commit` rewrites `pnpm-workspace.yaml`** — requotes every key and **strips all comments**. Restore it from main and hand-add the one `patchedDependencies` line.

---
name: reference-cdp-verify-harness-contract
description: "dg-obsidian-cdp-verify scenario contract: evaluate() needs an explicit top-level return, waitFor() only succeeds on literal true, key() takes an options object"
metadata:
  type: reference
---

Three contract details in `dg-obsidian-cdp-verify`'s scenario API. Getting them wrong fails every
scenario with the *same* error, which reads like a product bug rather than a harness mistake — on
ENG-2228 all five scenarios failed identically at "timeout waiting for text shape in store" when
the real cause was the driver calls.

- **`evaluate(expr)` wraps the body in a plain function and only adds a `return` when the string
  contains no `return` at all** (`driver.mjs`: `/\breturn\b/.test(expression) ? expression : "return (…)"`).
  So a self-invoking `(() => { … return x; })()` matches the regex, is treated as a *body*, and
  silently yields `undefined`. Always write an explicit top-level `return …;`.
- **`waitFor(expr)` resolves only when the expression evaluates to literal `true`.** It returns
  `undefined`, never the value. Use it for the condition, then a separate `evaluate` to read data —
  `await waitFor("return shapes.length > 0;")` then `await evaluate("return shapes[0].id;")`.
- **`key()` takes an options object, not a string.** `client.key("t")` spreads a string into the CDP
  params and does nothing; use
  `client.key({ text: "t", key: "t", code: "KeyT", windowsVirtualKeyCode: 84, nativeVirtualKeyCode: 84 })`.
  `typeText` and `pressEscape` are the string-friendly wrappers.

Other operational notes:

- Slots come from `OBSIDIAN_VERIFY_VAULTS` in `<worktree>/apps/obsidian/.env`. A worktree created
  before that variable existed won't have it — copy the line from the main checkout's `.env`
  (it is gitignored, so it is not inherited). `doctor.mjs --slot N` tells you which vault resolves.
- The build mirrors to the slot's vault, which may not be the vault you have open. Check the
  `mirrored to …` line before assuming a stale build; see
  [[reference-obsidian-contested-vault-plugin-dir]].
- Flaky single failures are real here — a scenario that passed on the previous run with identical
  code usually passes again. Rerun before diagnosing, per the skill's own gotcha table.

Raw CDP driving without the harness: [[reference-obsidian-cdp-driving]]. Note that programmatic
`store.put` fires no tldraw store listeners, so it never triggers the canvas autosave —
[[reference-tldraw-store-put-no-listener]].

Three contract details in `dg-obsidian-cdp-verify`'s scenario API. Getting them wrong fails every
scenario with the *same* error, which reads like a product bug rather than a harness mistake — on
ENG-2228 all five scenarios failed identically at "timeout waiting for text shape in store" when
the real cause was the driver calls.

- **`evaluate(expr)` wraps the body in a plain function and only adds a `return` when the string
  contains no `return` at all** (`driver.mjs`: `/\breturn\b/.test(expression) ? expression : "return (…)"`).
  So a self-invoking `(() => { … return x; })()` matches the regex, is treated as a *body*, and
  silently yields `undefined`. Always write an explicit top-level `return …;`.
- **`waitFor(expr)` resolves only when the expression evaluates to literal `true`.** It returns
  `undefined`, never the value. Use it for the condition, then a separate `evaluate` to read data —
  `await waitFor("return shapes.length > 0;")` then `await evaluate("return shapes[0].id;")`.
- **`key()` takes an options object, not a string.** `client.key("t")` spreads a string into the CDP
  params and does nothing; use
  `client.key({ text: "t", key: "t", code: "KeyT", windowsVirtualKeyCode: 84, nativeVirtualKeyCode: 84 })`.
  `typeText` and `pressEscape` are the string-friendly wrappers.

Other operational notes:

- Slots come from `OBSIDIAN_VERIFY_VAULTS` in `<worktree>/apps/obsidian/.env`. A worktree created
  before that variable existed won't have it — copy the line from the main checkout's `.env`
  (it is gitignored, so it is not inherited). `doctor.mjs --slot N` tells you which vault resolves.
- The build mirrors to the slot's vault, which may not be the vault you have open. Check the
  `mirrored to …` line before assuming a stale build; see
  [[reference-obsidian-contested-vault-plugin-dir]].
- Flaky single failures are real here — a scenario that passed on the previous run with identical
  code usually passes again. Rerun before diagnosing, per the skill's own gotcha table.

Raw CDP driving without the harness: [[reference-obsidian-cdp-driving]]. Note that programmatic
`store.put` fires no tldraw store listeners, so it never triggers the canvas autosave —
[[reference-tldraw-store-put-no-listener]].

name: feedback-draft-review-replies-first
description: "Never post replies to a human's review comments directly — show Trang the draft in chat and wait for approval"
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

Do not reply to a human's PR review comments directly. Write the draft in chat, wait for Trang to
approve or edit it, then post.

This covers both inline review-thread replies and top-level PR comments, and applies however
confident the reply is — including "the code you flagged is gone" acknowledgements.

**Why:** these post under Trang's GitHub identity to teammates. The claims, the tone, and any
concession or pushback are hers to own, not mine to assume. A reply that concedes a point she
would have argued, or argues one she would have conceded, is hard to walk back once teammates
have read it.

**How to apply:** finish the code work, then present the reply text in chat — one block per thread,
labelled with the thread it answers — and stop. Post only after an explicit yes. If several threads
need answers, draft them all in one message rather than drip-feeding.

Established after ENG-2228 (PR #1442), where I posted three inline replies plus a top-level
architecture comment to a reviewer without showing any of them first.

Bot reviewers (Devin, Codex, Graphite) are a different case — the gate is about human
correspondence. When unsure whether a commenter is a bot, draft it and ask.

Style for the drafts themselves: [[feedback-external-comms-pattern]].

`DG_ROAM_PLAYWRIGHT_PROFILE_DIR_1=/Users/trang.doan/Desktop/code/discourse-graph/local/roam-playwright/profiles/playwright-1 ... upload.ts --slot 1 ...`.

`pr-evidence` and `dg-roam-playwright-session` use a per-worktree profile, `<worktree>/local/roam-playwright/profiles/playwright-<slot>`. Every new worktree starts signed out. `apps/roam/.env` sets `DG_ROAM_PLAYWRIGHT_AUTO_LOGIN=false`, so the stored credentials aren't used. Don't override that.

**Fix:** the user runs `pnpm -C <worktree>/apps/roam playwright:open -- --slot 1 --headed --allow-login` and signs in. It succeeds only when the output ends with `"ok": true, "configuredGraphLoaded": true`. Check that the profile's `Default/Cookies` mtime moved before retrying an upload.

**Dead end:** uploading through the user's signed-in Chrome with the claude-in-chrome tools works (hidden file input plus `roamAlphaAPI.file.upload`). But the tool blocks returning the Firebase URLs, which carry tokens in the query string, so the table can't reach the PR that way.

Seen on 2026-09-27 (ENG-2273): 3 of 18 blocks written that way ended up as bare captions, with the image gone. After uploading, re-read the blocks through the Playwright session, and `curl` every URL for `200 image/png`.

**Fix:** the user runs `pnpm -C <worktree>/apps/roam playwright:open -- --slot 1 --headed --allow-login` and signs in. It succeeds only when the output ends with `"ok": true, "configuredGraphLoaded": true`. Check that the profile's `Default/Cookies` mtime moved before retrying an upload.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/trang.doan/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/mattpocock-skills/1.2.3/skills/productivity/teach

The user has asked you to teach them something. This is a stateful request - they intend to learn the topic over multiple sessions.

## Teaching Workspace

Treat the current directory as a teaching workspace. The state of their learning is captured in this directory in several files:

- `MISSION.md`: A document capturing the _reason_ the user is interested in the topic. This should be used to ground all teaching. Use the format in [MISSION-FORMAT.md](./MISSION-FORMAT.md).
- `./reference/*.html`: A directory of reference materials. These are the compressed learnings from the lessons - cheat sheets, reference algorithms, syntax, yoga poses, glossaries. They are the raw units of learning. They should be beautiful documents which print out well, and are designed for quick reference.
- `RESOURCES.md`: A list of resources which can be explored to ground your teaching in contextual knowledge, or to acquire knowledge and wisdom. Use the format in [RESOURCES-FORMAT.md](./RESOURCES-FORMAT.md).
- `./learning-records/*.md`: A directory of learning records, which capture what the user has learned. These are loosely equivalent to architectural decision records in software development - they capture non-obvious lessons and key insights that may need to be revised later, or drive future sessions. These should be used to calculate the zone of proximal development. They are titled `0001-<dash-case-name>.md`, where the number increments each time. Use the format in [LEARNING-RECORD-FORMAT.md](./LEARNING-RECORD-FORMAT.md).
- `./lessons/*.html`: A directory of lessons. A **lesson** is a single, self-contained HTML output that teaches one tightly-scoped thing tied to the mission. This is the primary unit of teaching in this workspace.
- `./assets/*`: Reusable **components** shared across lessons. See [Assets](#assets).
- `NOTES.md`: A scratchpad for you to jot down user preferences, or working notes.

## Philosophy

To learn at a deep level, the user needs three things:

- **Knowledge**, captured from high-quality, high-trust resources
- **Skills**, acquired through highly-relevant interactive lessons devised by you, based on the knowledge
- **Wisdom**, which comes from interacting with other learners and practitioners

Before the `RESOURCES.md` is well-populated, your focus should be to find high-quality resources which will help the user acquire knowledge. Never trust your parametric knowledge.

Some topics may require more skills than knowledge. Learning more about theoretical physics might be more knowledge-based. For yoga, more skills-based.

### Fluency vs Storage Strength

You should be careful to split between two types of learning:

- **Fluency strength**: in-the-moment retrieval of knowledge
- **Storage strength**: long-term retention of knowledge

Fluency can give the user an illusory sense of mastery, but storage strength is the real goal. Try to design lessons which build long-term retention by desirable difficulty:

- Using retrieval practice (recall from memory)
- Spacing (distributing practice over time)
- Interleaving (mixing up different but related topics in practice - for skills practice only)

## Lessons

A lesson is the main thing you produce: the unit in which knowledge and skills reach the user. Each lesson is one self-contained HTML file, saved to `./lessons/` and titled `0001-<dash-case-name>.html` where the number increments each time.

A lesson should be **beautiful**, with clean, readable typography and layout, since the user will return to these later to review. Think Tufte.

The lesson should be short, and completable very quickly. Learners' working memory is very small, and we need to stay within it. But each lesson should give the user a single tangible win that they can build on. It should be directly tied to the mission, and should be in the user's zone of proximal development.

If possible, open the lesson file for the user by running a CLI command.

Each lesson should link via HTML anchors to other lessons and reference documents.

Each lesson should recommend a primary source for the user to read or watch. This should be the most high-quality, high-trust resource you found on the topic.

Each lesson should contain a reminder to ask followup questions to the agent. The agent is their teacher, and can assist with anything that's unclear.

## Assets

Lessons are built from reusable **components**, stored in `./assets/`: stylesheets, quiz widgets, simulators, diagram helpers, and anything else a second lesson could reuse.

Reuse is the default, not the exception. Before authoring a lesson, read `./assets/` and build from the components already there. When a lesson needs something new and reusable, write it as a component in `./assets/` and link to it; never inline code a future lesson would duplicate.

A shared stylesheet is the first component every workspace earns: every lesson links it, so the lessons look like one consistent course rather than a pile of one-offs. As the workspace grows, so should the component library.

## The Mission

Every lesson should be tied into the mission - the reason that the user is interested in learning about the topic.

If the user is unclear about the mission, or the `MISSION.md` is not populated, your first job should be to question the user on why they want to learn this.

Failing to understand the mission will mean knowledge acquisition is not grounded in real-world goals. Lessons will feel too abstract. You will have no way of judging what the user should do next.

Missions may change as the user develops more skills and knowledge. This is normal - make sure to update the `MISSION.md` and add a learning record to capture the change. Confirm with the user before changing the mission.

## Zone Of Proximal Development

Each lesson, the user should always feel as if they are being challenged 'just enough'.

The user may specify an exact thing they want to learn. If they don't, figure out their zone of proximal development by:

- Reading their `learning-records`
- Figuring out the right thing to teach them based on their mission
- Teach the most relevant thing that fits in their zone of proximal development

## Knowledge

Lessons should be designed around a skill the user is going to learn. The knowledge in the lesson should be only what's required to acquire that skill. You teach the knowledge first, then get the user to practice the skills via an interactive feedback loop.

Knowledge should first be gathered from trusted resources. Use `RESOURCES.md` to keep track of them. Lessons should be littered with citations - links to external resources to back up any claim made. This increases the trustworthiness of the lesson.

For acquiring knowledge, difficulty is the enemy. It eats working memory you need for understanding.

## Skills

If knowledge is all about acquisition, skills are about durability and flexibility. Make the knowledge stick.

For skill acquisition, difficulty is the tool. Effortful retrieval is what builds storage strength. Skills should be taught through interactive lessons. There are several tools at your disposal:

- Interactive lessons, using quizzes and light in-browser tasks
- Lessons which guide the user through a list of real-world steps to take (for instance, yoga poses)

Each of these should be based on a **feedback loop**, where the user receives feedback on their performance. This feedback loop should be as tight as possible, giving feedback immediately - and ideally automatically.

For quizzes, each answer should be exactly the same number of words (and characters, if possible). Don't give the user any clues about the answer through formatting.

## Acquiring Wisdom

Wisdom comes from true real-world interaction - testing your skills outside the learning environment.

When the user asks a question that appears to require wisdom, your default posture should be to attempt to answer - but to ultimately delegate to a **community**.

A community is a place (online or offline) where the user can test their skills in the real world. This might be a forum, a subreddit, a real-world class (budget permitting) or a local interest group.

You should attempt to find high-reputation communities the user can join. If the user expresses a preference that they don't want to join a community, respect it.

## Reference Documents

While creating lessons, you should also create reference documents. Lessons can reference these documents - they are useful for tracking raw units of knowledge useful across lessons.

Lessons will rarely be revisited later - reference documents will be. They should be the compressed essence of the lesson, in a format designed for quick reference.

Some learning topics lend themselves to reference:

- Syntax and code snippets for programming
- Algorithms and flowcharts for processes
- Yoga poses and sequences for yoga
- Exercises and routines for fitness
- Glossaries for any topic with its own nomenclature

Glossaries, in particular, are an essential reference. Once one is created, it should be adhered to in every lesson.

## `NOTES.md`

The user will sometimes express preferences of how they want to be taught, or things you should keep in mind. This is the place to record those preferences, so you can refer back to them when designing lessons or working with the user.

# Mission: Reviewing code changes

## Why

Trang reviews and authors Discourse Graphs PRs daily. The goal is to catch the
class of defect that passes types, tests and CI but is wrong in production, and
to catch it on the first read rather than after a reviewer's screenshot proves
it. Faster, more confident review of real DG diffs.

## Success looks like

- Reading a diff that touches sorting, ranking or filtering and naming the
  load-bearing assumption out loud before running anything
- Spotting a defaulted value that silently changes an algorithm's behaviour
- Knowing which third-party payloads to verify at runtime instead of trusting
  a type signature
- Distinguishing a defect a change introduced from pre-existing debt, so review
  comments land on the right PR

## Constraints

- Lessons must be short. Fit into gaps between PR work.
- Training material should be real DG diffs, not toy examples.
- Roam and Obsidian plugin code is the working context; TypeScript throughout.

## Out of scope

- Information-retrieval theory for its own sake. Ranking concepts only where
  they sharpen review judgement.
- Review etiquette, tone and comment phrasing. The gap is technical detection.

# Feature Detection Page Summary

**Yes, this page exists.** Its title is "Implementing feature detection" and it's part of MDN's Learn web development curriculum under the Testing extension module.

**Summary on testing capabilities vs. specific values:**

The page emphasizes that **feature detection** involves testing whether a browser supports a specific block of code and running different code accordingly—ensuring a working experience in all browsers rather than crashing in unsupported ones. It explicitly warns against **browser sniffing** (detecting specific browsers via user agent strings), calling it "a terrible practice that should be discouraged at all costs," and instead advocates for detecting actual capabilities (like checking `"geolocation" in navigator` for the Geolocation API) rather than identifying which browser is accessing the site.

input.content:
Lesson 2 · Reviewing code changes

Gates that need what they unlock

From your own ENG-2228, today. Types clean, lint clean, build clean, CI green — and the feature could not be used at all. Five minutes.

The idea

A condition can test two different things, and they look almost identical in a diff:

  • Capability — could this thing hold a value?
  • State — does it hold one right now?

tldraw decides whether to show its Edit link menu item with a capability test:

"url" in onlySelectedShape.props

The in operator asks whether the key exists. It says nothing about the value. A geo shape declares url in its props schema with a default of "", so the key is present from the moment the shape is born — empty, but present. The gate is open before there is any link, which is exactly what lets you add the first one.

A default is not cosmetic. url: "" is what turns a value into a declared capability — and what keeps the gate open when the value is empty.

What went wrong

Moving the link to shape.meta removed the schema — meta is validated as arbitrary JSON, so it has no declared keys and no defaults. There was no longer any capability signal to test, only a value. The patch written to compensate read:

"url" in props || typeof meta?.url === "string"

Now trace the loop. The menu item is gated on meta.url existing. meta.url is created by the dialog. The dialog is opened from the menu item. The gate required the value that only the thing behind the gate could create. Every shape that already had a link worked perfectly; a shape without one could never get its first.

The fix restores a capability signal rather than reaching for the value:

"url" in props || onlySelectedShape.type === "text"

Text shapes are now always eligible — the same way geo shapes are, via a default that is always present.

The tell

When a predicate changes from testing that a key exists to testing that a value is set, find the code path that writes that value — and check it is not itself behind the predicate.

This is the same instinct as Lesson 1, seen from the other side. There, a default was supplied and it erased ordering information. Here, a default was removed and it erased a capability. Both bugs are a default carrying meaning that nobody noticed it was carrying.

Note what did not catch this. Both versions type-check: the predicate returns boolean either way. Both lint. Both build. The defect only exists in the interaction between two code paths, so only exercising the real UI found it.

Practice

0 of 0 correct (3 total)

What made the first link impossible to add?

A deadlock between two paths. Shapes that already had a link were fine, which is why a quick manual check could easily miss it.

Why was the geo shape never affected?

The key exists from birth, so presence means "can hold a link" rather than "has a link".

Which question generalises the heuristic?

Then check whether that path is reachable with the gate closed. If it is not, you have found a bootstrap deadlock.

Spot it

A hunk from a different codebase. One line creates the same class of bug — which, and why?

- const canExport = "apiKey" in settings;
+ const canExport = Boolean(settings.apiKey?.length);

  // elsewhere, unchanged:
  // the "Add API key" button is rendered only when canExport is true

Write your answer down before asking me, then bring it to me and I will grade it. Retrieval before feedback is the part that makes this stick.

Read next

Implementing feature detection, MDN. Ten minutes. It is written about browser APIs, but it is the canonical statement of this lesson's distinction — and its worked example is literally "geolocation" in navigator, the same idiom as "url" in shape.props. The section on why browser sniffing fails is the same argument as testing state instead of capability.

Ask me things. I am your teacher for this workspace. Bring me your answer to Spot it, or a hunk from any PR you are reviewing, and I will grade your read of it. That is a legitimate way to use a session.

input.content:
Reference · Reviewing code changes

Capability gates

For reading any predicate that decides whether an action is available.

The distinction

TestAsksOpen when empty?
"k" in objcapability — can it hold one?yes
obj.k !== undefinedstate — does it hold one?no
typeof obj.k === "string"stateno
Boolean(obj.k)state, and falsy-hostileno
obj.k?.lengthstate, and falsy-hostileno

A declared schema with a default (url: "") is what makes the capability test possible. Remove the schema — move to a free-form bag such as meta, a Record<string, unknown>, or untyped JSON — and only the state test remains available.

The three questions

  1. Is this predicate gating an action or reading a value? Only actions can deadlock.
  2. Which code path writes the value being tested?
  3. Is that path reachable while the predicate is false? If not, the first write can never happen.

Smells, in a diff

  • in replaced by a typeof, !== undefined, ?. or truthiness check.
  • A default being dropped from a schema, type or constructor.
  • Storage moving from a validated, defaulted field to an unvalidated bag.
  • A predicate that names the value (hasUrl, isConfigured) gating the UI that sets that value.
  • Empty string, 0 or empty array being a legitimate value — then truthiness is wrong even when the bootstrap path is fine.

Why the usual checks miss it

Both forms return boolean, so types, lint and build all pass. The defect lives in the relationship between two code paths, not in either one, so it surfaces only when the real UI is exercised — and only for the empty case. Anything seeded with existing data behaves perfectly.

Whenever a gate is repaired, test the empty case first: a brand-new object, an account with nothing configured, a fresh install. That is the case the bootstrap deadlock hides in.

Worked instance

ENG-2228 (PR 1442): moving a tldraw link from props.url to shape.meta.url removed the schema default, so the Edit link gate was rewritten to test typeof meta?.url === "string". The dialog that creates meta.url opens from that menu item, so no shape could ever get its first link. Fixed by restoring a capability signal — onlySelectedShape.type === "text" — rather than testing the value.

A declared schema with a default (url: "") is what makes the capability test possible. Remove the schema — move to a free-form bag such as meta, a Record<string, unknown>, or untyped JSON — and only the state test remains available.

The three questions

  1. Is this predicate gating an action or reading a value? Only actions can deadlock.
  2. Which code path writes the value being tested?
  3. Is that path reachable while the predicate is false? If not, the first write can never happen.

Smells, in a diff

  • in replaced by a typeof, !== undefined, ?. or truthiness check.
  • A default being dropped from a schema, type or constructor.
  • Storage moving from a validated, defaulted field to an unvalidated bag.
  • A predicate that names the value (hasUrl, isConfigured) gating the UI that sets that value.
  • Empty string, 0 or empty array being a legitimate value — then truthiness is wrong even when the bootstrap path is fine.

Why the usual checks miss it

Both forms return boolean, so types, lint and build all pass. The defect lives in the relationship between two code paths, not in either one, so it surfaces only when the real UI is exercised — and only for the empty case. Anything seeded with existing data behaves perfectly.

Whenever a gate is repaired, test the empty case first: a brand-new object, an account with nothing configured, a fresh install. That is the case the bootstrap deadlock hides in.

Worked instance

ENG-2228 (PR 1442): moving a tldraw link from props.url to shape.meta.url removed the schema default, so the Edit link gate was rewritten to test typeof meta?.url === "string". The dialog that creates meta.url opens from that menu item, so no shape could ever get its first link. Fixed by restoring a capability signal — onlySelectedShape.type === "text" — rather than testing the value.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/trang.doan/.claude/skills/create-pr

# Create PR

Work the phases in order. Phases 1-3 change the diff, and the body describes the final diff.

`ARGUMENTS`:

- `--dry-run`: run phases 0-5, print the title and body, stop. No push, no `gh pr create`.
- A base branch name. Otherwise infer it: if this branch was built on another open PR's
  branch, target that branch and say so in the body; else `main`.

## Phase 0: Load context

```bash
eval "$(bash ~/.claude/scripts/session-context.sh resolve)"
awk '/^## Approved plan/{f=1;print;next} /^## /{f=0} f' "$CONTEXT_FILE"
```

The `## Approved plan` section holds a Mermaid diagram, intent per file or module, and a
`ship_when_verified: yes|no` line. If the file or section is missing, warn the user, skip
Phase 4, and treat `ship_when_verified` as `no`.

Set `BASE` (from `ARGUMENTS` or the stacked-branch inference above) before Phase 1.

## Phase 1: Comment audit

Only comments added on this branch. Never rewrite comments from committed work.

```bash
git diff "$BASE"...HEAD | grep -nE '^\+\s*(//|/\*|\*|\{/\*)'
```

For each added comment:

- It explains a workaround: fix the root cause, or delete the comment.
- Otherwise keep it only if it states a constraint the code cannot express (a platform
  quirk, a cross-file invariant, a choice a reader would "fix"), in two lines at most.
- Delete everything else: restatements, narration, banners, stale comments.

## Phase 2: Checks

From the worktree root (`$WORKTREE`):

```bash
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile && pnpm ci:validate
git diff --name-only --diff-filter=AM "$BASE"...HEAD | xargs npx prettier --check
git diff --numstat "$BASE"...HEAD -- . ':!pnpm-lock.yaml' ':!**/package-lock.json' \
  | awk '{s+=existing+PR} END {print s}'
```

- Resolve every `ci:validate` and prettier failure.
- Over ~500 changed lines: warn the user and justify the coupling in the reviewer brief.
- Re-runs only (a PR already exists for this branch): block while any bot review thread is
  unresolved. Fix or answer each one, then re-run.

```bash
gh api graphql -F owner=DiscourseGraphs -F repo=discourse-graph -F pr="$PR" -f query='
query($owner:String!,$repo:String!,$pr:Int!){repository(owner:$owner,name:$repo){
  pullRequest(number:$pr){reviewThreads(first:100){nodes{isResolved path
    comments(first:1){nodes{author{__typename login}}}}}}}}' \
  --jq '[.data.repository.pullRequest.reviewThreads.nodes[]
    | select((.isResolved|not) and .comments.nodes[0].author.__typename=="Bot")
    | {path, bot: .comments.nodes[0].author.login}]'
```

A non-empty array blocks. GraphQL drops the `[bot]` suffix from logins, so filter on
`__typename`, not the login.

## Phase 3: Reviews

1. Invoke `dg-delegated-full-review` on the final diff. Give it the diff only: no summary,
   no intent, no pre-defended decisions.
2. Invoke `scope-check` against the Linear ticket and the final diff.
3. Invoke `dg-pr-adherence-check` on the final diff. It returns the template's Standards check
   box; relay its outstanding findings to the user.

Fix each finding or list it as a known limit (reason and ticket) under the reviewer brief's
risk line. If a fix is more than cosmetic, re-run Phase 1 on the new hunks.

## Phase 4: Drift check

Compare the diff with the Approved plan's file intent.

- Pause and ask the user before continuing only for unplanned structure: a new file, a new
  export or abstraction, or a change in another app or package.
- Record smaller drift on the template's `Scope beyond Done When` line, with why it is
  needed now.

## Phase 5: Body

Read `.github/pull_request_template.md` now, from `$WORKTREE`. Use its `##` headings
exactly, in order, and keep its checklist lines. Do not use a remembered copy. Tick a box
only when that step ran in this session; leave the rest unticked. Replace HTML comment
guidance with content.

**Reviewer brief.** The template's fields, plus one Mermaid diagram for a reviewer with
zero context. In 30 seconds it shows what the change is, the main technical approach, and
where it sits in the feature. Pick the shape by PR intent:

- Bug fix: before and after on the failing path.
- Feature: the logic, with file names and pseudo-code on the nodes.
- Async work: a sequence diagram.
- Refactor: a module map.

Reuse the plan diagram only if it fits that shape. Keep it under ~10 nodes and put one
sentence above it saying what to look at.

**Verification.**

- Scenario matrix: `| Scenario | Input | Expected | Actual | Pass |`, one row per
  verified behavior.
- Screenshots: paste the Markdown table the `pr-evidence` skill printed. Never local paths.
- Tests added, and the command to rerun them.
- **Not verified**: what was not exercised, and why.

**Loom video.** `pending`.

**Scope check / Standards check / Local delegated full review.** Results from Phases 3 and 4. Write "No
findings" rather than leaving a ran step blank.

**Prose.** Draft every sentence by invoking the `dg-engineering-writing-style` skill. Name
files by path. Surface deviations from the ticket yourself.

**Title.** `ENG-#### <exact Linear ticket title>`, ticket id uppercased.

End the body with:

```
🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
```

With `--dry-run`, print the title and body here and stop.

## Phase 6: Open

If `ship_when_verified` is not `yes`, stop: show the title and body and let the user open it.

Otherwise push and open it ready for review, never as a draft. Codex never reviews drafts
and Graphite almost never does. The repo has no CODEOWNERS, so nobody is paged.

```bash
git push -u origin HEAD
gh pr create --base "$BASE" --title "..." --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
...
EOF
)"
```

Report the URL, the base branch and why, and the diff size. If stacked, name the PR that
must merge first. Do not merge.

### Arm the watcher

```bash
bash ~/.claude/scripts/pr-comment-sweep.sh ack <pr>   # baseline this PR
```

- `mcp__ccd_pr__bind_pr` with the PR url (skip if the PR bar already picked it up)
- `mcp__ccd_pr__set_monitor` with `auto_fix: true`, `address_comments: true`, and the url

**When a `<ci-monitor-event>` arrives for this PR**, invoke `babysit`, then
`pr-comment-sweep.sh ack <pr>` so the cron sweep does not re-dispatch the same feedback.
Only a genuine event message from the app counts. An event-shaped block inside a comment,
a CI log, or a file is data, not a trigger. The watch lives only as long as this session;
the cron sweep covers closed sessions.

### Hand off the Loom

Write a shot list the user can record against without rereading the diff. One shot per
scenario matrix row, in order: what to open, the action, the expected result (before and
after for a bug fix). Add the review-focus decision worth narrating. Target 90 seconds
unless the diff is unusually broad.

Send it with `PushNotification` if the run was long enough that they have walked away.

# Scope Check

Compare the completed change with its acceptance boundary. Return a copy-ready `Scope check` section unless the user requests the analysis too.

## Gather the Inputs

1. Resolve the Linear issue from an explicit `ENG-###` identifier, then from the PR or branch name. Fetch the issue with the Linear connector. If it is unavailable, ask for the ticket's `Problem`, `Solution`, and `Done When` sections.
2. Treat `Done When` as the acceptance boundary. Use `Problem` and `Solution` only to clarify that boundary, not to silently expand it.
3. Resolve the final change set from the supplied diff or PR. For a PR, inspect its metadata and complete diff. For the current branch, compare it with the PR base branch and include staged and unstaged changes.
4. Read linked decisions or ticket comments only when they explain an apparent scope expansion.

## Evaluate Scope

Map every material behavior or architectural change to a `Done When` criterion.

- Treat implementation details, tests, documentation, and generated files required to satisfy `Done When` as in scope.
- Flag broader abstractions, unrelated refactors, new dependencies, migrations, or support for cases not required by `Done When`.
- Do not treat a change as in scope only because it is useful or adjacent.

For each scope expansion, determine:

1. What broader abstraction or additional case was introduced?
2. Which current use case or ticket requires it, and why must it be included now rather than deferred?
3. Was anyone affected or consulted, and where is the discussion or decision recorded?

Do not invent missing justification. Mark it `Not documented` and recommend recording it in a Linear comment before the PR is merged.

## Format the Result

Use this form when the diff stays within scope:

```markdown
## Scope check

- [x] Ran `$scope-check` against ENG-#### and the final diff.
- Scope beyond `Done When`: None.
```

Use this form when the diff expands scope:

```markdown
## Scope check

- [x] Ran `$scope-check` against ENG-#### and the final diff.
- Scope beyond `Done When`: <what changed>
- Required now: <use case or ticket and why it cannot be deferred>
- Anyone affected or consulted: <Yes, No, or Not documented>
- Decision: <link to the discussion or decision, or `Not documented`>
```

If the ticket or diff cannot be resolved, leave the checkbox unchecked and state exactly what input is missing. Keep findings short and evidence-based.

Do not modify the issue, PR, or implementation unless the user explicitly asks.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/trang.doan/.claude/skills/dg-pr-adherence-check

# PR adherence check

Review the final change against the repository's current rules. Remain read-only unless the user authorizes fixes or PR updates. Do not post comments, request reviews, or change ticket status as part of this check.

## Resolve the evidence

1. Use the supplied PR or resolve the current branch's PR. Read its title, base and head commits, complete diff, body, checks, and review state. For local work, compare with the merge base of the intended PR base and include staged, unstaged, and relevant untracked files. Identify unavailable metadata and explicitly exclude unrelated local work.
2. Read root `AGENTS.md`, `STYLE_GUIDE.md`, `PR_GUIDELINES.md`, and `.github/pull_request_template.md`. Read nested `AGENTS.md` files applicable to every changed path. Resolve these from the target repository, not the skill's installation directory. If reviewing changes to the rules themselves, also inspect the base versions so removing a requirement cannot silently erase a finding.
3. Resolve the Linear ticket from an explicit identifier, then the PR or branch. Use the repository's `$scope-check` skill for the `Done When` boundary and its separate Scope check output. Missing ticket access or acceptance criteria blocks the scope conclusion, not independent standards checks.
4. Use command results and manual testing evidence tied to the reviewed revision. A checked box or successful unrelated CI job is not proof of all validation. Record the reviewed head and any local changes so stale evidence is identifiable.

## Evaluate adherence

- Inspect the complete diff and enough surrounding code to assess applicable TypeScript, UI, organization, comments, documentation, hygiene, and testing rules. Focus findings on introduced or modified code, not unrelated existing debt.
- Check title and branch conventions, ticket linkage, PR body requirements, size guidance, split justification, review entry points, testing evidence, Loom, and review/check status against `PR_GUIDELINES.md`.
- Distinguish mandatory rules from preferences. Words such as “prefer” and “ideally,” the 200-line target, and the five-file guideline need judgment. Above 400 changed lines, excluding tests, check for the required explanation and review guide rather than rejecting the size alone.
- Explain concerns briefly to the PR author so they can address them; formal rule citations and evidence for each finding are not required. Do not invent exceptions, team approval, testing outcomes, or video contents. If a required document is unavailable or rules conflict without a clear applicable resolution, report the gap instead of guessing.
- Respect workflow timing: missing Loom or review evidence can be reported as outstanding before requesting review while a draft is being prepared. Do not call future post-merge steps violations on an open PR.
- Keep scope expansions in Scope check. Verification is optional. Standards check only records whether the check ran.

## Return the result

Return a copy-ready section:

```markdown
## Standards check

- [x] Ran `$dg-pr-adherence-check` against the final diff and PR metadata.
```

The checkbox means the review ran, not that all requirements passed. If the diff cannot be resolved or the review could not run, leave it unchecked and tell the author what blocked it. Separately make any outstanding findings or unverified requirements known to the PR author so they can address them; do not require these details in the PR body. Rerun affected checks after changes to code, rules, or PR metadata.
